questiontext.text:
In the proof above that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational, the fraction \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) is chosen in its simplest form. Which of these statements about that choice are correct? Select all that apply.

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Choosing \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) in its simplest form costs nothing: every rational number can be written that way, by cancelling common factors, as in \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). It is also essential. Showing that \(p\) and \(q\) are both even is not impossible in itself (6 and 4 are both even); it is impossible for a fraction in its simplest form. So the contradiction is with the choice of \(\dfrac{p}{q}\), and the proof rules out every fraction: if \(\sqrt{2}\) were equal to any fraction, it would be equal to one in its simplest form.

The correct statements are the second and the fourth. The first is false: any fraction equal to \(\sqrt{2}\) could be cancelled down to one in its simplest form, and the proof shows that there is no such fraction. The third is false: two integers can both be even, and the contradiction is only with the choice of a fraction in its simplest form.

questionvariables.text: ta1: [[c_only, false, "The proof shows only that \\(\\sqrt{2}\\) is not a fraction in its simplest form; a fraction such as \\(6/4\\) could still equal \\(\\sqrt{2}\\)."], [c_every, true, "Every rational number can be written as a fraction in its simplest form, so this choice does not leave out any rational number."], [c_both, false, "The contradiction is that \\(p\\) and \\(q\\) are both even, which is impossible for any two integers."], [c_need, true, "The contradiction comes from this choice: the proof shows that \\(p\\) and \\(q\\) are both even, so \\(p/q\\) could not have been in its simplest form."]];

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 8.1 (Solution 8.1, pp. 37-38) in Section 8 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Correct. The choice costs nothing, and it is exactly what the proof contradicts.

node.description: Diagnostic: only fractions in simplest form ruled out

truefeedback.text: Any fraction can be cancelled down to its simplest form: \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). So if \(\sqrt{2}\) were equal to some fraction, it would be equal to one in its simplest form, and the proof shows that this is impossible. The proof rules out every fraction.

node.description: Diagnostic: both even taken as impossible in itself

truefeedback.text: Two integers can perfectly well both be even: 6 and 4 are. What is impossible is a fraction in its simplest form with an even numerator and an even denominator.

falsefeedback.text: Two of the statements are correct. Ask what would go wrong if \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) were not in its simplest form, and whether choosing it in its simplest form loses anything.

qtest.description: Only one of the two correct statements
